title: Memory, identity and loss: Poppies, War Photographer, The Emigrée and Checking Out Me History
specPoints: Paper 2 Section B: Power and Conflict: Poppies, War Photographer, The Emigrée, Checking Out Me History
AO2: voice, imagery and form; AO3: identity and memory

tips.title: Four people not fighting
tips.body: A mother (Poppies); a photographer and his readers (War Photographer); an emigrant (The Emigrée); a man and his history (Checking Out Me History).

tips.title: Images that carry war
tips.body: Sewing words in Poppies; religious words in War Photographer; light in The Emigrée and Checking Out Me History.

tips.title: Pairs to prepare
tips.body: Poppies with War Photographer or Kamikaze; The Emigrée with Checking Out Me History or Tissue.

tips.title: Readings, held lightly
tips.body: The son in Poppies may be dead or only gone; say what the dove and the memorial allow.

why.matters: These poems widen what conflict means: the fear of a family at home, the guilt of comfortable readers, the loss of a homeland, and the fight over whose history is taught. June 2024 asked how people are affected by conflict, and its indicative content named these poems for the effects on those not directly involved and on identity. They give an answer to almost any question a second poem that is not about a battlefield.

examples.title: Photographs of war
examples.body: Pictures of suffering from distant wars are shared, moved past and forgotten in minutes. Duffy wrote War Photographer about newspaper supplements in 1985, and its question about who pictures of suffering are for has become more urgent, not less.

examples.title: Whose history?
examples.body: Arguments about which people and events are taught in schools, and which are left out, are still going on. Checking Out Me History is one person's answer: find your own heroes and carve out your own identity.

steps.title: Poppies: a mother and a son who has gone
steps.body:
Jane Weir wrote *Poppies* in 2009, at the request of the Poet Laureate, Carol Ann Duffy, who asked poets to respond to the wars of the time, including the war in Afghanistan. It is in copyright, so it is quoted in short phrases.

**The situation.** A mother speaks to her son as he leaves home, apparently for the army. It begins “Three days before Armistice Sunday”, when she pins a poppy on his blazer.

**Domestic images, war images.** The poppy's petals are “spasms of paper red”, against “a blockade of yellow bias binding”: sewing words, with war words inside them. She rolls “Sellotape bandaged around my hand” to take the cat hair off his collar.

**Holding back.** She wants to smooth his hair and does not. “I was brave”. He leaves; for him “the world overflowing like a treasure chest”.

**After.** She goes to a war memorial; she sees “the dove pulled freely against the sky”; she ends “hoping to hear your playground voice catching on the wind”.

rows: A bird; peace, or a spirit leaving
props.title: Poppies

visuals.alt: A table of four images from Poppies and the two meanings in each

check.prompt: Why does Weir mix sewing words with war words, as in a blockade of yellow bias binding?
check.solution: Bias binding is a sewing tape; a blockade is a military barrier. Every domestic detail carries a trace of war, so the reader feels her fear without her naming it.

markScheme.description: The mother's domestic world is invaded by the war her son is going to, so her ordinary care carries fear

options: Because the mother is a seamstress who makes uniforms for the army and is sewing her son's blazer on the morning he leaves for his first day at a new school in the town
Because the poem is about sewing
Because Weir liked fabric
The mother's domestic world is invaded by the war her son is going to, so her ordinary care carries fear

steps.title: War Photographer: the pictures and the reader
steps.body:
Carol Ann Duffy published *War Photographer* in 1985. A photographer is alone in his darkroom in England, developing the photographs he took in war zones. It is in copyright, so it is quoted in short phrases.

**A priest.** The darkroom is like a church, the photographer like a priest; his films are “spools of suffering set out in ordered rows”. The cities are listed like a prayer: “Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh.” “All flesh is grass”.

**Detachment and its limit.** “He has a job to do”; “solutions slop in trays”; but his hands tremble now, at home, though they did not there.

**England and the war zones.** At home, fields do not explode beneath “running children in a nightmare heat”.

**The reader.** The pictures go to a newspaper supplement. “The reader's eyeballs prick with tears” between the bath and pre-lunch beers; “they do not care”.

boxes.title: The darkroom
boxes.body: A church; spools in ordered rows

boxes.title: The photographer
boxes.body: He has a job to do

visuals.alt: Four boxes on War Photographer: the darkroom, the photographer, the contrast, and the reader

check.prompt: What does the ending, they do not care, suggest about the photographer's work?
check.solution: The readers' eyeballs prick with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers, and then they do not care. The poem turns its criticism on comfortable readers, and on the reader of the poem.

markScheme.description: The suffering he records moves readers only briefly, and then is forgotten

options: The suffering he records moves readers only briefly, and then is forgotten
That the newspaper editors do not care about the quality of his photographs and print them badly, which is why he is so angry in the darkroom when the prints come out
That he does not care
That the war has ended

steps.title: The Emigrée: a city carried in memory
steps.body:
Carol Rumens published *The Emigrée* in 1993. The speaker left her country as a child and has never gone back; the city is never named. It is in copyright, so it is quoted in short phrases.

**Opening like a story.** “There once was a country”: the phrase sounds like a fairy tale. “I left it as a child”, and remembers it “sunlight-clear”.

**Memory against news.** She knows the city now may be at war: “It may be sick with tyrants”. But “I am branded by an impression of sunlight”.

**The city as a person.** “my city takes me dancing”; “My city hides behind me”. It is loved like a companion and protected like a secret.

**Why unnamed.** Without a name, it could be any city someone has had to leave. Memory has made it hers alone.

rows: A memory that cannot be removed
props.title: The Emigrée

visuals.alt: A table of four lines from The Emigrée and what each shows

check.prompt: Why is branded a powerful choice in I am branded by an impression of sunlight?
check.solution: Branding marks for ever, and often painfully. The memory of sunlight is burned into her, a comfort and a wound at once.

markScheme.description: A brand is burned in and permanent, so the bright memory is fixed and cannot be removed, whatever the city has become

options: Because the speaker works in advertising and has designed a brand for the city, using the sun as a logo, which is why she describes it as sunlight-clear and bright
A brand is burned in and permanent, so the bright memory is fixed and cannot be removed, whatever the city has become
Because it means she is sunburnt
Because it is a happy word

steps.title: Checking Out Me History: a history taken back
steps.body:
John Agard was born in Guyana, in the Caribbean, and moved to Britain. The poem is written in a Caribbean English, a Creole, not in standard spelling. It is in copyright, so it is quoted in short phrases.

**The accusation.** “Dem tell me”, over and over: the history he was taught, “Dem tell me bout 1066 and all dat”, Dick Whittington, Florence Nightingale.

**The blindfold.** “Bandage up me eye with me own history”; “Blind me to me own identity”. Taught history hid his own.

**His heroes.** Set apart, in italic sections, figures from Black and Caribbean history: “Toussaint L'Ouverture”, who led the revolution in Haiti; Nanny de Maroon; “Mary Seacole”, who nursed soldiers in the Crimea and was called “a healing star”, “a yellow sunrise”.

**The ending.** He will be “carving out me identity”: identity made by choosing your own history.

visuals.alt: A table of the history Agard was taught and the history he found for himself

check.prompt: Why does Agard set his heroes in italic sections with different rhythms?
check.solution: The taught history comes in the insistent Dem tell me lines; his heroes come in lyrical italic sections with images of light and healing. Form separates the imposed from the chosen.

markScheme.description: The change of form marks a different, freer history set apart from the one imposed on him

options: Because the italic parts were written by a different poet, whom Agard asked to contribute to the poem because she knew more about Caribbean history than he did
Because italics are easier to read
The change of form marks a different, freer history set apart from the one imposed on him
For no reason

steps.title: Comparing Poppies and War Photographer
steps.body: Two poems about people not in the fighting, which the June 2024 indicative content named for the effects of conflict on those not immediately involved.

visuals.problem: Compare how poets present people affected by conflict from a distance.

steps.text: Idea: both show conflict reaching people far from it, but Weir shows love that cannot let go and Duffy shows attention that lets go too easily.
steps.note: A comparative claim with a turn.

steps.text: Poppies: domestic images carry war: “spasms of paper red”; “a blockade of yellow bias binding”.
steps.note: The war inside a mother's care.

steps.text: War Photographer: religious images carry suffering: “spools of suffering set out in ordered rows”; “All flesh is grass”.
steps.note: The war inside a darkroom ritual.

steps.text: Endings: the mother “hoping to hear your playground voice catching on the wind”; the readers' eyes prick with tears and then “they do not care”.
steps.note: Grief that lasts against sympathy that does not.

steps.text: Judgement: Weir asks us to feel with the mother; Duffy accuses the reader. Duffy's ending is harder, because it includes us.

check.prompt: Which sentence judges the difference between the two endings?
check.solution: The sentence about grief and accusation compares both endings and says which is harder and why. The others describe a likeness or one detail.

markScheme.description: Weir's ending holds on to grief, while Duffy's accuses the reader of letting go, which makes Duffy's the harder ending

options: Poppies ends at a war memorial
War Photographer ends in England
Both poems end sadly, because both are about war and both describe people who are upset about what has happened to someone they love who has gone away to fight
Weir's ending holds on to grief, while Duffy's accuses the reader of letting go, which makes Duffy's the harder ending

steps.title: Identity: The Emigrée and Checking Out Me History
steps.body:
Two poems where conflict is between a person and what others say about who they are.

**The Emigrée** holds on to a remembered city against the news: “I am branded by an impression of sunlight”.

**Checking Out Me History** takes back a history against the one taught: “carving out me identity”.

**Voice.** Rumens's speaker is lyrical and private; Agard's is defiant and spoken aloud, in Creole, a choice that is itself part of the argument.

**Light.** Both use light for what they value: sunlight-clear, a healing star, a yellow sunrise. Compare the method and its purpose.

The June 2024 indicative content named *Tissue* and *The Emigrée* for the effects of conflict on attitudes and sense of identity.

visuals.alt: A table comparing The Emigrée and Checking Out Me History

check.prompt: What do the two poems share in their use of light?
check.solution: Sunlight-clear and branded by sunlight in The Emigrée; a healing star and a yellow sunrise in Checking Out Me History. The same image, used to value what power would take away.

markScheme.description: Both use light for what the speaker values and keeps: a remembered city, heroes found for himself

options: Both use light for what the speaker values and keeps: a remembered city, heroes found for himself
Both use light to show danger
Both are set at dawn, and both describe the sun rising over a city at war, which is why the speakers are able to see the soldiers and the tanks in the streets below them
Neither uses light

steps.title: Plan: Poppies and Kamikaze
steps.body:
Try: *Compare how poets present the effects of conflict on families in 'Poppies' and in 'Kamikaze'.*

1. The idea: families pay for war twice, in fear and in silence.
2. Voice: a mother speaking to her son; a daughter retelling her father's story.
3. Images: sewing and war; the sea and the dark prince.
4. Endings: listening for a voice; the better way to die.
5. Context: Afghanistan and 2009; Japan in the Second World War.

Then write the paragraph on voice.

check.prompt: What is the key difference in voice between Poppies and Kamikaze?
check.solution: Poppies uses second-person address to the absent son, intimate and present; Kamikaze reports at a generation's distance, until the daughter's own voice breaks in.

markScheme.description: Poppies is a mother speaking directly to her son; Kamikaze is a daughter retelling her father's story to her own children

options: Poppies is spoken by the son, who describes his mother pinning the poppy on him, and Kamikaze is spoken by the pilot himself, as he flies towards the enemy ships
Poppies is a mother speaking directly to her son; Kamikaze is a daughter retelling her father's story to her own children
Both are spoken by soldiers
Neither has a speaker

steps.title: Context and interpretation
steps.body:
**Weir, 2009.** Written as British soldiers were serving in Afghanistan; the poem's son is never named and his fate is never stated. Is he dead, or just gone? The poem allows both.

**Duffy, 1985.** Duffy was inspired by a friendship with war photographers; the poem asks who a picture of suffering is for.

**Rumens, 1993.** Written after decades of refugees from wars and dictatorships; the unnamed city could be anywhere.

**Agard.** A Guyanese poet in Britain, writing against a school history that left out people like him.

Hold the readings lightly and ground them in words: the dove, they do not care, sick with tyrants, carving.

rows: The son may be dead, or only gone

check.solution: The explored reading holds two possibilities and grounds both in images. The certain reading overstates; the others stop at the surface.

steps.title: Memory, identity and loss in one page
steps.body:
Four poems about people changed by conflict they did not fight.

- **Poppies (Weir, 2009):** a mother, a son leaving; sewing and war images; I was brave; the dove; a playground voice.
- **War Photographer (Duffy, 1985):** a darkroom like a church; spools of suffering; running children; they do not care.
- **The Emigrée (Rumens, 1993):** a city left as a child; sick with tyrants; branded by sunlight; my city takes me dancing.
- **Checking Out Me History (Agard):** Dem tell me; bandage up me eye; Toussaint, Nanny, Mary Seacole; carving out me identity.
- **Pairs:** Poppies with War Photographer or Kamikaze; The Emigrée with Checking Out Me History or Tissue.

questions.prompt: Compare how poets present the effects of conflict on those not directly involved in 'Poppies' and 'War Photographer'. Write the opening idea and one integrated paragraph.
questions.solution: Both poems show conflict reaching people far from it, but Weir shows a love that cannot let go while Duffy shows an attention that lets go too easily. Both carry war inside a quiet domestic or professional ritual. Weir's mother tidies her son before he leaves, and the language of her care is shot through with war: the poppy is “spasms of paper red”, the tape on his blazer “a blockade of yellow bias binding”, the Sellotape “Sellotape bandaged around my hand”. Duffy's photographer develops his prints like a priest at a service, his films “spools of suffering set out in ordered rows”, the cities recited, “Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh.” Where Weir's imagery makes the reader feel the mother's fear, Duffy's makes the reader feel judged: the mother ends “hoping to hear your playground voice catching on the wind”, her grief still open, while the newspaper's readers feel their eyeballs prick with tears and then “they do not care”. Weir, writing in 2009 while British soldiers served in Afghanistan, asks the reader to grieve with a family; Duffy turns the poem on the reader, which makes hers the harder ending, because the indifference it describes is ours.

questions.prompt: Write one analytical paragraph on how Agard presents identity in 'Checking Out Me History'.
questions.solution: Agard presents identity as something taken back from the people who defined it. The repeated accusation “Dem tell me” introduces the history he was taught, “Dem tell me bout 1066 and all dat”, Dick Whittington and Florence Nightingale, and the metaphors show what it did to him: “Bandage up me eye with me own history”, “Blind me to me own identity”. The bandage that should heal instead blinds. Against this he sets the history he found, in italic sections with a softer, lyrical rhythm: “Toussaint L'Ouverture”, Nanny de Maroon, and “Mary Seacole”, who is “a healing star” and “a yellow sunrise”. The change of form separates the imposed history from the chosen one, and the Creole voice throughout refuses the standard English of the classroom. A poet born in Guyana, writing in Britain, Agard ends by claiming the right to make himself: “carving out me identity”, a verb of effort and craft, as if identity were cut from stone.

examTechnique.body:
**Know who is affected.** A mother, a photographer, readers, an emigrant, a pupil taught the wrong history.

**Short, exact lines.** All four are in copyright and only the named poem is printed.

**Compare images and endings.** Sewing and religion; light; a voice listened for, indifference, a city kept, an identity carved.

**Context in a sentence.** 2009 and Afghanistan; 1985 and newspaper supplements; refugees; a Guyanese poet in Britain.
examinerErrors: Retelling the situation instead of analysing voice and imagery.
Stating that the son in Poppies is dead as a fact.
Missing that War Photographer criticises readers.
Treating Agard's Creole as a mistake rather than a choice.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer on these poems sees conflict beyond the battlefield, compares images and voices, offers readings held lightly and grounded in words, and ties context to lines: a mother's fear in 2009, a reader's indifference, a memory kept against tyranny, a history taken back.
